questions.q: What precisely distinguishes a reinforcement-learning problem from solving a Markov decision process by dynamic programming?
choices: RL uses a discount factor and MDPs do not
In RL the transition kernel P and reward R are unknown and must be learned from sampled interaction
RL has no states, only actions
RL requires the environment to be deterministic
questions.explain: An RL problem is an MDP whose model — the transition kernel $P(s'\mid s,a)$ and reward $R(s,a)$ — is unknown. Value/policy iteration assume the model is given; RL instead learns optimal behaviour from sampled transitions $(s,a,r,s')$.

questions.q: Under an ε-greedy policy with ε = 0.1 in a state with 4 available actions, what is the probability the greedy (currently best) action is taken?
questions.explain: With probability $1-\varepsilon=0.9$ you take the greedy action outright, and with probability $\varepsilon=0.1$ you choose uniformly among all $4$ actions, which includes the greedy one with probability $1/4$. Total $= 0.9 + 0.1\cdot\tfrac14 = 0.9 + 0.025 = 0.925$.

questions.q: Select every statement that correctly describes the exploration–exploitation tradeoff and the on/off-policy distinction.
choices: Pure exploitation can lock onto a suboptimal action whose true value was never sampled
Off-policy methods can learn about a target policy while behaving under a different (exploratory) policy
On-policy methods evaluate and improve the same policy that generates the data
Exploration is unnecessary once any reward has been observed
questions.explain: Exploitation alone risks committing to an action whose value estimate is high only by chance, so some exploration is needed for consistency. Off-policy learning separates the behaviour policy (which explores) from the target policy being learned; on-policy learning ties them together. Statement 4 is false — a single observed reward says nothing about untried alternatives.

questions.q: An episode visits state $s$ then observes the reward sequence $r_1 = 1,\ r_2 = 0,\ r_3 = 2$ before terminating, with discount $\gamma = 0.5$. What is the sampled return $G$ used to update $V(s)$?
questions.explain: $G = r_1 + \gamma r_2 + \gamma^2 r_3 = 1 + 0.5\cdot 0 + 0.25\cdot 2 = 1 + 0 + 0.5 = 1.5$. Monte Carlo uses this complete discounted return as its (unbiased) sample of $V^\pi(s)$.

questions.q: Why is the Monte Carlo estimate of $V^\pi(s)$ — the average of sampled returns from $s$ — an unbiased estimator?
choices: Because it bootstraps from the current value estimates
Because each sampled return $G_t$ is itself a draw whose expectation given $s_t=s$ is exactly $V^\pi(s)$
Because it requires knowing the transition kernel P
Because $\gamma$ is set to 1
questions.explain: By definition $V^\pi(s)=\mathbb E_\pi[G_t\mid s_t=s]$, so each observed return is a sample whose mean is the target. Averaging samples is therefore unbiased — and crucially uses no model of $P$ or $R$. (Unlike TD, MC does not bootstrap.)

questions.q: What is the difference between first-visit and every-visit Monte Carlo for estimating $V^\pi(s)$?
choices: First-visit averages the return only from the first time s is reached in each episode; every-visit averages from all visits
First-visit uses γ = 0 and every-visit uses γ = 1
First-visit is off-policy and every-visit is on-policy
There is no difference
questions.explain: First-visit MC averages the return following only the first occurrence of $s$ within each episode; every-visit MC averages the returns following every occurrence. Both converge to $V^\pi(s)$ as the number of visits grows.

questions.q: Apply one TD(0) update. Currently $V(s) = 2$ and $V(s') = 5$. The agent observes reward $r = 1$ on the transition $s \to s'$, with $\gamma = 0.9$ and step size $\alpha = 0.1$. What is the TD error $\delta = r + \gamma V(s') - V(s)$?
questions.explain: $\delta = r + \gamma V(s') - V(s) = 1 + 0.9\cdot 5 - 2 = 1 + 4.5 - 2 = 3.5$. The update is then $V(s)\leftarrow V(s)+\alpha\delta = 2 + 0.1\cdot 3.5 = 2.35$.

questions.q: What does it mean to say TD(0) 'bootstraps', and how does that contrast with Monte Carlo?
choices: TD waits for the episode to end; MC updates every step
TD updates toward a target r + γV(s′) built from its own current estimate; MC updates toward the full sampled return
TD requires the model P; MC does not
They are identical when γ = 0
questions.explain: Bootstrapping means the update target $r+\gamma V(s')$ reuses the current value estimate $V(s')$ rather than waiting for the actual return. Monte Carlo instead targets the complete sampled return $G_t$, which needs the episode to finish. This is the bias (TD) vs. variance (MC) tradeoff.

questions.q: At the true value function $V^\pi$, what is the expected TD error $\mathbb E[\delta] = \mathbb E[r + \gamma V^\pi(s') - V^\pi(s)]$ for a transition out of state $s$ under policy π?
choices: Strictly positive
Zero
Equal to γ
Undefined
questions.explain: The Bellman expectation equation says $V^\pi(s)=\mathbb E[r+\gamma V^\pi(s')]$, so $\mathbb E[\delta]=\mathbb E[r+\gamma V^\pi(s')]-V^\pi(s)=0$. The true value is exactly the TD fixed point: on average there is nothing left to correct.

questions.q: Apply one Q-learning update. Currently $Q(s,a) = 4$. The agent takes $a$, gets reward $r = 2$, and lands in $s'$ where $Q(s',a_1') = 3$ and $Q(s',a_2') = 7$. With $\gamma = 0.5$ and $\alpha = 0.1$, what is the new $Q(s,a)$ after the update $Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha[r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)]$?
questions.explain: The bootstrapped target uses $\max_{a'}Q(s',a')=\max(3,7)=7$: target $= r+\gamma\cdot 7 = 2 + 0.5\cdot 7 = 5.5$. Then $Q(s,a)\leftarrow 4 + 0.1\,(5.5-4) = 4 + 0.1\cdot 1.5 = 4.15$.

questions.q: What is the precise difference between the Q-learning and SARSA update targets?
choices: Q-learning uses $\max_{a'} Q(s',a')$ (off-policy); SARSA uses $Q(s',a')$ for the action $a'$ actually taken next (on-policy)
Q-learning has no discount factor; SARSA does
SARSA uses the max and Q-learning uses the actual action
They differ only in the learning rate α
questions.explain: Q-learning bootstraps off the greedy action $\max_{a'}Q(s',a')$ regardless of what the behaviour policy does — off-policy. SARSA (state-action-reward-state-action) bootstraps off the action $a'$ the agent actually takes next under its current policy — on-policy.

questions.q: Q-learning's convergence to $Q^*$ is justified by stochastic-approximation theory. Which condition on the step sizes $\alpha_t$ (Robbins–Monro) is required?
choices: $\alpha_t$ must be constant for all t
$\sum_t \alpha_t < \infty$ and $\sum_t \alpha_t^2 = \infty$
$\sum_t \alpha_t = \infty$ and $\sum_t \alpha_t^2 < \infty$
$\alpha_t$ must increase over time
questions.explain: The Robbins–Monro conditions $\sum_t\alpha_t=\infty$ (steps large enough to reach anywhere) and $\sum_t\alpha_t^2<\infty$ (steps shrink fast enough to average out sampling noise) make Q-learning a stochastic approximation to the fixed point of the Bellman-optimality operator — the same $\gamma$-contraction that drives value iteration, now driven by samples.

questions.q: The 'deadly triad' names three ingredients whose combination can make value-based RL diverge. Select the three.
choices: Bootstrapping (TD-style targets that reuse the current estimate)
Off-policy training (learning a target policy from data generated differently)
Function approximation (a parametric value function rather than a table)
Using a discount factor γ < 1
questions.explain: The deadly triad is bootstrapping + off-policy training + function approximation. Each alone is fine; together the contraction guarantee can fail and the parameters can diverge. A discount $\gamma<1$ is benign — indeed it is what makes the tabular operator a contraction.

questions.q: Why move from a tabular Q to a parametric $Q(s,a;w)$ with semi-gradient TD?
choices: To guarantee convergence in every setting
To generalize value estimates across states when the state space is too large or continuous to enumerate
Because tables cannot store negative values
To eliminate the need for a reward signal
questions.explain: A lookup table needs one entry per state(-action), which is hopeless for large or continuous spaces. A parametric approximator shares parameters so that experience at one state informs nearby states — generalization, the same concern as empirical risk minimization in statistical learning. (It comes at the cost of the convergence guarantees the tabular case enjoys.)

questions.q: Deep Q-networks (DQN) stabilize off-policy training with function approximation primarily by using:
choices: A larger discount factor
Experience replay and a slowly-updated target network
Removing the max operator
Switching to first-visit Monte Carlo
questions.explain: DQN mitigates the deadly triad in practice with an experience-replay buffer (decorrelating samples and reusing data) and a separate target network whose weights are held fixed for many steps (stabilizing the bootstrap target). Neither removes the divergence risk in theory, but together they make deep value learning workable.

questions.q: The policy-gradient theorem gives $\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb E_{\pi_\theta}[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a\mid s)\, Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)]$. What does REINFORCE use in place of $Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)$?
choices: The known transition kernel P
The sampled (Monte Carlo) return $G_t$ from that state-action onward
The maximum over actions of Q
A fixed constant
questions.explain: REINFORCE is the Monte Carlo policy-gradient method: it replaces the unknown $Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a)$ with the actual sampled return $G_t$, giving the unbiased estimator $\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\,G_t$ that needs no model.

questions.q: Subtracting a state-dependent baseline $b(s)$ to form $\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a\mid s)\,[Q^{\pi_\theta}(s,a) - b(s)]$ has what effect on the gradient estimate?
choices: It introduces bias but lowers variance
It leaves the estimate unbiased and typically reduces its variance
It always increases the variance
It changes the optimal policy
questions.explain:
Because $\mathbb E_a[
abla_	heta\log\pi_	heta(a\mid s)\,b(s)] = b(s)\,
abla_	heta\sum_a\pi_	heta(a\mid s)=b(s)\,
abla_	heta 1 = 0$, the baseline adds zero in expectation: the estimator stays unbiased. A well-chosen $b(s)$ (e.g. $\approx V^{\pi_	heta}(s)$) shrinks the magnitude of the multiplier and so reduces variance.

questions.q: What distinguishes an actor–critic method from plain REINFORCE?
choices: Actor–critic removes the policy and keeps only a value function
Actor–critic uses a learned value function (the critic) as the baseline / bootstrap, while the actor is the parameterized policy
Actor–critic requires a known model P
Actor–critic can only be applied to deterministic policies
questions.explain: Actor–critic keeps the parameterized policy (the actor) but replaces the Monte Carlo return with an estimate from a learned value function (the critic), which serves as the baseline and lets the actor update from incomplete episodes via bootstrapping — combining policy gradients with TD-style value learning.
